title: The Optimist Is Made, Not Born
essay_markdown:
Optimism isn't a mood you wait for. It's something you do.

Michael J. Fox learned this the hard way. He was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease when he was just 30 years old. Years later, after a run of painful health setbacks unrelated to Parkinson's, he hit bottom. In a 2020 People cover story, he described leaning against his kitchen wall while waiting for an ambulance, feeling there was no bright side to any of it. His way back came from remembering his late father-in-law, a man who always talked about gratitude. Fox began noticing things he was thankful for. He later told AARP The Magazine, "I concluded that gratitude makes optimism sustainable." He also said that "You can't wait for things to be great and then be grateful for that. You've got to behave in a way that promotes that."

Today's idea is simple: be optimistic and positive, because life is too short to be negative. That doesn't mean pretending things are fine. Fox doesn't pretend. He openly says "Some days are a struggle. Some days are more difficult than others." Optimism is about where you put your attention once you've looked honestly at what's in front of you.

"Life is too short" turns out to be literally true here. A 2019 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences followed 69,744 women from the Nurses' Health Study and 1,429 men from the Veterans Affairs Normative Aging Study. The most optimistic men and women lived 11 to 15% longer on average, and had 50-70% greater odds of reaching 85 years old compared to the least optimistic groups. The researchers admit it is unclear how exactly optimism helps people attain longer life. One possibility is that optimistic people tend to have healthier habits. Either way, a negative outlook doesn't just make your days feel worse. It may also be linked to having fewer of them.

So here's the reframe Fox points to: treat optimism as a set of actions, not a feeling. You can't order yourself to feel hopeful. You can change what you say, what your face does, and what you choose to laugh at. Feelings tend to catch up.

Start with complaining. In 2006, Will Bowen was teaching a class on prosperity at a small church in Kansas City, and he handed out purple rubber bracelets. The rule was that participants would switch their bracelet with every spoken complaint to the other wrist, and keep switching until they'd gone 21 consecutive days without complaining. Bowen himself struggled with it: "I moved my bracelet so many times that I broke three of them before making it 21 consecutive days." The lesson is that most of us have no idea how often we grumble. We complain about the slow coffee line, the traffic, or the meeting that could have been an email. Venting now and then is human. The habit worth breaking is the automatic one. When you catch yourself, follow the complaint with a question: what can I actually do about this?

Next, smile. Smile at the barista, the neighbor in the elevator, or the tired cashier at the end of their shift. Many people will smile back, and even the ones who don't have still been offered a little warmth.

Then laugh, especially at yourself. Laugh at the coffee you spilled on your shirt, the email you sent to the wrong person, and the toddler-level tantrum you nearly threw over a printer jam. Most mistakes are funnier than they are tragic once you step back far enough to see them.

Here's how to practice today:

- **Put something on your wrist.** A hair tie or rubber band works. Switch wrists each time you complain out loud, and after every switch, name one small action you could take instead.
- **Smile at the first three people you see,** strangers included.
- **Look for gratitude tonight.** Before bed, follow Fox's lead and find one thing you're grateful for. If nothing comes to mind, "keep looking".

You don't have to wake up feeling optimistic. You just have to start doing what optimists do, and today is a good day to begin.

item.title: Be Optimistic / Positive
item.body: For life is too short to be negative.

subitems.title: Don’t complain
subitems.body: Complaining generates all this negative energy that makes you no different than an energy vampire. While it’s okay to vent occasionally, be conscious of the times when you do that. Cut down on the time you spend complaining and think about what you can do about the situation instead.

subitems.title: Smile
subitems.body: How often do you smile a day? Smiling is something we don’t do enough. Whether you’re out on the streets or at work, it’s more common to see people with stoic expressions and hard frowns than smiles. The next time you see someone, even a stranger, smile at them. You’ll be surprised how many people will return the smile. Even if they don’t, trust that they have been warmed by your smile.

subitems.title: Laugh
subitems.body: As they say, laughter is the best medicine. Learn to laugh at the jokes people make, at the obstacles you’re facing, at the mistakes you’re making, and at the mystery that is life.
